scope: Five original AQA AS Physics Waves 3.3.1.2, 3.3.1.3 and 3.3.2.2 applications (33 marks), including two genuine sketches
notes: Original exercises, not published AQA questions or official mark schemes. Real drawing evidence earns no automatic keyword marks, and other equivalent written working and ECF require manual review. Polarisation questions exclude Malus's law; no laboratory operating instructions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA AS Waves Polarisation, Stationary and Diffraction
questions.question: Sketch third-harmonic standing-wave snapshots and phase
questions.subtopic: Phase and stationary waves, polarisation and slit diffraction
questions.prompt: A string fixed at x=0 and x=0.90 m vibrates in its third harmonic. The wave speed is 120 m s⁻¹. Draw a labelled displacement-versus-position sketch at maximum displacement, another after half a period, and state what the string looks like after a quarter period. Mark all nodes and antinodes. Explain the phase relationship in adjacent loops and calculate the frequency. [8 marks]
markPoints: Draws a three-loop stationary-wave pattern with alternating adjacent loop displacement signs.
Labels nodes at x=0, 0.30, 0.60 and 0.90 m.
Labels antinodes at x=0.15, 0.45 and 0.75 m.
Shows the half-period snapshot with the displacement of every loop inverted while node positions remain fixed.
Explains after a quarter of a period from maximum displacement the whole string passes through its equilibrium line.
States points within a single loop oscillate in phase.
States neighbouring loops oscillate in antiphase (180° out of phase).
questions.modelAnswer: The third harmonic has 3 loops. Nodes are at 0, L/3=0.30, 2L/3=0.60 and L=0.90 m; antinodes are midway at 0.15, 0.45 and 0.75 m. At one maximum-displacement instant the loops alternate +,−,+; after T/2 they alternate −,+,−. After T/4 from maximum displacement all points pass the equilibrium line. Points within a loop oscillate in phase; points in neighbouring loops are 180° apart. λ=2L/3=0.60 m, hence f=v/λ=120/0.60=200 Hz. Sketches must be manually reviewed.
questions.questionType: graphical wave sketch requiring manual review

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA AS Waves Polarisation, Stationary and Diffraction
questions.question: Polarisation, Polaroid filters and receiving aerials
questions.subtopic: Phase and stationary waves, polarisation and slit diffraction
questions.prompt: A linearly polarised radio wave has its electric-field oscillations vertical. A straight receiving aerial is used to pick up this wave. Explain its best orientation and why rotating it through 90° reduces the ideal received signal. A beam of light passes through two ideal crossed polarising sheets. State what emerges and explain what these examples demonstrate about the wave oscillations. Do not use Malus's law. [5 marks]
markPoints: Identifies the wave as transverse and states its electric-field oscillation is perpendicular to propagation.
States the receiving aerial should be vertical, aligned with the electric-field direction.
Explains a horizontally oriented aerial couples poorly to the vertical electric field in the idealised model.
States ideal polarising sheets with transmission axes at 90° transmit no light after the second sheet.
Explains polarisation selects a vibration direction and provides evidence of transverse rather than longitudinal oscillations.
questions.modelAnswer: The electric field of an EM wave oscillates transverse to the direction of travel. For a vertically polarised radio wave, a straight vertical aerial is aligned with this oscillating field, giving the strongest ideal reception. Turning the aerial horizontal reduces coupling to a vertical field. Two ideal crossed Polaroid sheets have perpendicular transmission axes, so no light emerges after the second. Polarisation shows that the wave has transverse oscillations; the intensity law for intermediate angles is not required.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA AS Waves Polarisation, Stationary and Diffraction
questions.question: Compare qualitative single-slit fringe patterns
questions.subtopic: Phase and stationary waves, polarisation and slit diffraction
questions.prompt: Draw a qualitative screen pattern of bright and dark fringes for monochromatic light passing through a single narrow slit. Label the central bright maximum and the weaker side maxima on both sides. On a second screen-pattern sketch show what changes when the slit width is reduced at fixed wavelength. Explain the change and state how an increased wavelength affects the central maximum. Do not plot an intensity-versus-angle graph. [6 marks]
markPoints: Sketch shows a clearly broader, brighter central fringe than adjacent side fringes.
Sketch shows weaker side fringes on both sides of the central fringe.
Indicates dark regions/minima separating the bright fringes.
Second screen-pattern sketch shows a broader central fringe for a narrower slit.
Explains the decreased slit width increases the angular spread/diffraction.
States longer wavelength at fixed slit width also widens the central bright fringe.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw a screen strip with a wide, bright central fringe, weaker and narrower bright side fringes, and dark regions between them. On a second strip, show the central fringe becoming wider when the slit is narrowed. The angular spread increases as slit width decreases; at a fixed width a longer wavelength also gives a wider central maximum. AQA does not require an intensity-versus-angle graph. All drawn fringe patterns are reviewed manually.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA AS Waves Polarisation, Stationary and Diffraction
questions.question: String harmonic frequency and squared-frequency gradient
questions.subtopic: Phase and stationary waves, polarisation and slit diffraction
questions.prompt: A string has vibrating length L=0.800 m and mass per unit length μ=0.640 g m⁻¹. (a) Convert μ to SI units. (b) Calculate the first-harmonic frequency at tension T=16.0 N using f=(1/2L)√(T/μ). (c) Explain why f² against T is a straight line and calculate the theoretical gradient. (d) State the factor by which f changes if T rises from 16.0 N to 36.0 N. [7 marks]
markPoints: Converts μ=0.640 g m⁻¹ to 6.40×10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹.
Uses f=(1/(2L))√(T/μ) with consistent SI units.
Calculates f≈98.8 Hz for T=16.0 N.
Squares to obtain f²=T/(4L²μ), predicting a straight line through the origin.
Gives gradient 1/(4L²μ) for an f²-versus-T graph.
Calculates gradient ≈610 Hz² N⁻¹ (610.35 to additional figures).
Uses f∝√T to find ratio √(36.0/16.0)=1.50 (revised f≈148 Hz is also acceptable).
questions.modelAnswer: μ=0.640/1000=0.000640 kg m⁻¹. f=(1/(2×0.800))√(16.0/0.000640)=98.82 Hz, or 98.8 Hz to three significant figures. Squaring yields f²=T/(4L²μ), so plotting f² vertically against T horizontally gives a straight line through zero with gradient 1/(4×0.800²×0.000640)=610.35 Hz² N⁻¹≈610 Hz² N⁻¹. If tension rises 16.0 to 36.0 N, frequency multiplies by √(36/16)=1.50, becoming about 148 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA AS Waves Polarisation, Stationary and Diffraction
questions.question: Explain standing-wave formation from two opposite progressive waves
questions.subtopic: Graphical superposition and creation of stationary wave nodes
questions.prompt: Two coherent sinusoidal waves, each of amplitude A, frequency f and wavelength λ, travel along a string in opposite directions. At t=0 their displacements coincide. Sketch their individual displacements and resultant at t=0, then show their individual displacements and resultant after one-quarter period. Indicate node/antinode positions and explain how stationary waves arise. The diagrams require manual marking. [7 marks]
markPoints: Draws or identifies two progressive waves of the same frequency, wavelength and amplitude travelling in opposite directions.
Shows the two displacements add point by point using the superposition principle.
At t=0 shows an in-phase resultant of twice the amplitude (2A) where the waves align.
At t=T/4 shows opposite equal wave displacements and a straight equilibrium-line resultant.
Identifies node positions as fixed points of zero resultant displacement, separated by λ/2.
Identifies antinodes halfway between nodes, at maximum resultant amplitude.
Explains that successive superposed displacements at fixed positions form a stationary pattern with no overall movement of the nodes.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw two equal sinusoidal progressive waves travelling in opposite directions. At t=0, when their displacements coincide, their pointwise sum is a sinusoid of amplitude 2A; its zero-displacement node positions are fixed, half a wavelength apart, with antinodes midway. A quarter-period later the two waves have equal and opposite instantaneous displacements at every position, so their sum is zero everywhere. After a further quarter-period the pattern is inverted. This is superposition of equal-frequency opposite-travelling waves, giving a stationary-wave pattern; nodes do not travel along the string. Manually compare the two individual snapshots and their resultants before awarding any diagram points.
questions.questionType: graphical wave superposition with mandatory manual inspection
